name: recall-floors-v1
about: Synthetic: every person, place and fact is invented. Seven conversations of about 40 messages, each asked recall_probes after a given message, and three memory pools whose chats hold facts the user stated, asked shared_probes. A recall probe is scored against the conversation's older messages: those before the last recent_turns messages ahead of the probe, which the prompt already carries. A shared probe is scored against every item of its pool. relevant lists what holds the information the turn needs, the user's statement and the assistant's answer to it alike; every other candidate is irrelevant.

kinds.exact_restatement: The turn restates earlier wording, often with its numbers or identifiers.
kinds.paraphrase: The turn asks about an earlier exchange in other words, sharing no rare word with it.
kinds.follow_up: A short turn whose meaning comes from the recent turns; the earlier exchange it needs is labelled.
kinds.instruction_only: A request about the last answer, or thanks, with nothing behind it in the older messages.
kinds.distractor: A new topic that shares common words with old messages; nothing older bears on it.
kinds.shared_bearing: A turn that a fact the user stated in another chat of the pool bears on.
kinds.shared_unrelated: A turn that no item of the pool bears on.

messages.text: I started baking sourdough two weeks ago and my first loaf came out like a brick. I used 500g of bread flour, 350g of water, 10g of salt and about 100g of starter. What went wrong?

That recipe is fine, roughly 70% hydration, so the problem is probably underproofing or a weak starter. Does your starter double in size within six hours of feeding? A sluggish starter is the usual cause of a dense crumb.
I don't think it does. I fed it this morning and it has barely moved. My kitchen is only 17°C right now because the heating stays off during the day.
That explains it. At 17°C fermentation is very slow. Try the oven with just the light switched on, which sits around 25°C, and keep the starter there between feeds until it doubles reliably.
Good idea. How much should I feed it? At the moment I do 1:1:1 starter to flour to water, once a day, with plain white flour.
For a young starter in a cool kitchen, feed 1:2:2 twice a day, about every 12 hours. The extra flour and water dilute the acid and give the yeast fresh food before it runs out.
Done, I'll do 1:2:2 every 12 hours from tonight. Should I discard some first? I hate throwing so much away.
Yes, discard down to 50g before each feed, otherwise the amounts grow quickly. You can keep the discard in a jar in the fridge and use it for pancakes or crackers.
Pancakes it is. Four days later the starter doubles in about five hours and smells like yoghurt with a hint of apple. Is it ready to bake with?
That sounds ready. Use it at its peak, when it has doubled and the top is domed or just starting to flatten. A spoonful dropped in water should float.
It floats! I want to try a proper overnight loaf this weekend. I bought a 9-inch oval banneton and a cast iron Dutch oven. How should I schedule it?

Mix and autolyse for 45 minutes, add the salt, then do four sets of stretch and folds, one every 30 minutes. Shape, place in the floured banneton, and retard it in the fridge at 4°C for 12 to 14 hours.
What should I use to dust the banneton so the dough doesn't stick? Last time I used wheat flour and it glued itself on.
Use a half-and-half mix of rice flour and wheat flour. Rice flour does not absorb moisture, so it forms a non-stick layer that wheat flour alone cannot.
Rice flour, got it. Now the baking. What temperature for the Dutch oven?

Preheat the Dutch oven at 250°C for 45 minutes with the lid on. Load the cold dough, score it, bake 20 minutes at 230°C with the lid on, then 15 minutes with the lid off until the crust is deep brown.
What should I use to score it? I tried a kitchen knife and it dragged the dough.
A razor blade on a stick, called a lame, held at about 30 degrees to the surface. Cut quickly and about one centimetre deep. A cold, firm dough from the fridge cuts much more cleanly.
Baked it. Great oven spring and a lovely ear! But the crumb is a bit gummy in the middle. What does that mean?
Gummy crumb usually means the loaf was cut too early or slightly underbaked. Let it cool for at least an hour, and check that the internal temperature reaches 96°C before you take it out.
I did cut it after about 15 minutes, so that's probably it. I also want more flavour. Can I swap some of the white flour for something else?
Replace 20% of the white flour with stoneground wholemeal or rye. Both add flavour and ferment faster, so shorten your fridge time by an hour or two and watch the dough rather than the clock.
I'll try 20% rye. Also, I'm going away for nine days in October for my sister's wedding. What do I do with the starter while I'm gone?
Feed it, let it rise for an hour, then store it in a sealed jar in the fridge. It will be fine for nine days. When you return, give it two feedings at room temperature before baking.
Great. Could I dry some as a backup in case I kill it?
Yes. Spread a thin layer of active starter on baking paper, let it dry fully for a day or two, then crumble it into a jar. Rehydrate with equal weights of flour and water if you ever need it.
Dried flakes are saved in a jar. Okay, different question: how should I store the finished bread so it stays fresh?
Keep a cut loaf cut-side down on a board for the first day, then slice and freeze what you will not eat in two days. Plastic bags soften the crust, so a linen bag or bread bin is better.
Slicing and freezing sounds right. Does toasting from frozen work okay?
Yes, slices toast straight from the freezer; just add a minute. For a whole frozen loaf, thaw at room temperature for three hours and refresh it in a 200°C oven for ten minutes.
This weekend I want to bake a seeded loaf. Which seeds work well and how much should I use?

Use about 15% of the flour weight in total: sunflower, pumpkin and flax work well. Toast the seeds, then soak them in an equal weight of hot water for an hour so they don't steal moisture from the dough.
How would that change the hydration? 350g of water with 500g of flour felt right for the plain loaf.
Count the soaker's water in your total, since you drain nothing. Bump the main water down by roughly the soaked amount, then adjust by feel. A seeded dough should be tacky, not sticky.
The seeds are toasted and soaking right now. What would be a good topping for the crust?
Brush the shaped loaf with water and roll it in a tray of seeds before the fridge, so they stick. Oats or sesame work too, and they brown nicely in the lid-off phase.
Rolling it in oats then. The seeded loaf is baking and the smell is amazing.
Lovely. Remember to let it cool for a full hour before you cut. Seeds hold moisture, so a seeded crumb stays gummy-looking longer if cut warm.
Okay. I've noticed that my starter gets a layer of grey liquid on top when I forget it. Is it spoiled?
No, that liquid is hooch, a sign the starter is hungry. Pour it off or stir it in, then feed as normal. Only pink or orange streaks or fuzzy mould mean it should be thrown away.
One of our queries on the orders table takes about 12 seconds in production. It filters by customer_id and sorts by created_at descending, limit 50. The table has 40 million rows. Where do I start?
Start with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the exact query. If you see a sequential scan or a sort that spills to disk, an index on (customer_id, created_at DESC) will probably remove both.
Here's the plan: Seq Scan on orders, filter customer_id = 88213, rows removed by filter 39,998,112, then top-N heapsort. Execution time 11,904 ms.
That confirms it. Nearly the whole table is read to return a handful of rows. Create the composite index so Postgres can walk it in order and stop after 50 rows.
I ran CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC); it took 9 minutes and blocked writes. Is there a safer way?
Yes. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which does not take a lock that blocks writes. It is slower and cannot run inside a transaction, and if it fails it leaves an invalid index you must drop.
Understood. We're on PostgreSQL 16.3. After the index the query takes 3 ms, which is great. But another report query still takes forever: it counts orders per status.
A count over 40 million rows has to visit many pages. Check whether a partial or covering index helps, or keep a small summary table updated by a trigger or a periodic job.
Management is happy with approximate counts. Is there something cheaper?
For a whole-table estimate, read reltuples from pg_class. For a filtered one, use the row estimate from EXPLAIN or maintain a counter table. Both are instant but approximate.
Switching topics: we got ERROR: deadlock detected (SQLSTATE 40P01) twice last night from the nightly import. It updates inventory rows in whatever order the file lists them.

Classic cause: two transactions lock the same rows in different orders. Sort the rows by primary key before updating, or take locks with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in a fixed order, and keep transactions short.
I'll sort by sku_id first. Can I make the import retry automatically if a deadlock still occurs?
Yes. Deadlock errors (40P01) and serialization failures (40001) are safe to retry. Wrap the transaction in a retry loop with a few attempts and a short random backoff.
We also see too many connections errors. max_connections is 100 in /etc/postgresql/16/main/postgresql.conf and the app opens a pool of 40 per instance with 5 instances.
Five instances times 40 is 200, over your limit. Put PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode in front, shrink each app pool to about 10, and keep max_connections modest.
Should I just raise max_connections to 300 instead? It's one line.
Each connection costs memory, and work_mem is per sort operation per connection, so 300 connections can exhaust RAM. A pooler is the better fix; raise the limit only slightly as a stopgap.
Okay, PgBouncer it is. Our server has 32GB of RAM. What work_mem is sensible?
Start around 32 to 64MB for a pooled workload of about 50 active connections, then check temp file usage in pg_stat_database. Raise it per session for heavy reports rather than globally.
I set work_mem to 64MB. Now autovacuum: the orders table has bloated to 90GB while live data is about 55GB. Why?
Updates and deletes leave dead tuples. If autovacuum cannot keep up, or a long-running transaction holds back cleanup, bloat grows. Check pg_stat_user_tables for n_dead_tup and last_autovacuum.
n_dead_tup is 18 million. last_autovacuum was 3 days ago. There's also a reporting transaction that stays open for hours.

That open transaction is likely blocking cleanup. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and statement_timeout for the reporting role, and lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor for this table to 0.02.
Set the scale factor to 0.02 for orders. Will that shrink the file on disk?
No. Plain VACUUM makes space reusable but rarely returns it to the operating system. To shrink the file you need VACUUM FULL, which locks the table, or pg_repack, which works online.
We can't lock the table for hours. How would pg_repack work for us?
It builds a fresh copy of the table with a trigger capturing changes, then swaps it in with a brief lock. It needs free disk space roughly equal to the table size and a primary key.
We have enough disk. Next, I want to change orders.total from integer cents to numeric(12,2). Safe to do online?
ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock. Instead add a new column, backfill in batches, switch the application over, then drop the old column in a later release.
Backfill in batches of how many rows? We don't want replication lag.
Batches of 5,000 to 10,000 rows with a short sleep between them are typical. Watch replay lag on the replica and pause the job if it exceeds a few seconds.
Good. We use a read replica for reports; sometimes reports fail with 'canceling statement due to conflict with recovery'.

That is the replica cancelling queries that conflict with replayed changes. Set hot_standby_feedback = on, or raise max_standby_streaming_delay, accepting some replay delay or extra bloat on the primary.
I'll enable hot_standby_feedback. Different question: how do I find the slowest queries over the last week?

Enable the pg_stat_statements extension, then order by total_exec_time. It aggregates by normalized query, so you can see which statements cost the most overall rather than just the slowest single run.
pg_stat_statements is installed. The top query is an ORDER BY random() LIMIT 1 used for a 'random product' widget.
ORDER BY random() sorts the whole table. Pick a random id in the key range and select the next existing row, or use TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM for an approximate random row cheaply.
TABLESAMPLE sounds fine for a widget. Last thing: can I check which indexes we never use?
Query pg_stat_user_indexes for idx_scan = 0 since the last statistics reset, ignoring unique and primary key indexes. Check replicas too before dropping anything.
I signed up for a half marathon on March 14 and I've only ever run 5k. I can run three days a week, and I get up at 6am on weekdays, so mornings are best. How should I start?
With about 16 weeks to go, that is enough. Start with three runs a week: two easy runs of 30 minutes and one longer run that grows by about 10% a week. Keep easy runs conversational.
What does conversational pace mean in numbers? My 5k pace is around 6:10 per km.
Easy pace is usually 60 to 90 seconds per kilometre slower than 5k pace, so about 7:15 to 7:40 per km for you. If you can't speak in full sentences, slow down.
That feels painfully slow but I'll try. I'm running Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday. Should the long run be Sunday?
Yes, Sunday for the long run leaves Tuesday and Thursday for easy runs, with rest days between. Start the long run at 6 km and add 1 km each week, with a shorter recovery week every fourth week.
Week three update: my left knee aches after the Sunday long run, on the outside, just below the kneecap.

Lateral knee pain in new runners is often iliotibial band irritation from weak hips and a sudden mileage jump. Cut the next long run by 30%, add hip strength twice a week, and see a physio if it persists.
Which strength exercises? I only have a resistance band and a mat at home.
Try banded side steps, clamshells, single-leg glute bridges and step-ups on a sturdy stair. Two sets of 12 each, twice a week, after an easy run is plenty.
Doing those. I also need shoes. I've been running in old trainers from the cupboard. What should I look for?
Get fitted at a running shop. Look for a pair with enough cushioning for 30 to 40 km a week, a roomy toe box, and a comfortable fit. Buy half a size up since feet swell on long runs.
I bought a neutral cushioned pair, size 43. People say to rotate two pairs. Is that necessary?
Not necessary, but alternating two pairs can spread impact stress and lets the foam recover between runs. A second pair is worth it once your weekly mileage passes 30 km.
Week seven: long run is now 12 km and the knee is fine. How should I fuel on runs over 10 km?

Eat a carbohydrate-rich dinner the night before, a banana or toast an hour before, and for runs over 75 minutes take about 30 g of carbohydrate per hour: a gel or a few chews every 30 to 40 minutes with water.
I tried a gel at 8 km and my stomach cramped. Is that normal?
Common. Practise fuelling in training, start with half a gel, take it with water not sports drink, and try different flavours or chews. The gut adapts over several weeks.
Thanks. What about heart rate zones? My watch says my average on easy runs is 162, which seems high.

For many runners 162 is high for an easy pace. Estimate your maximum heart rate, around 190 for you, and aim for zone 2, roughly 125 to 150. If you are over, slow down or take walk breaks until the pace drops.
Maybe I'm just running too fast on the hills. The Thursday route has a long climb at 3 km.
Hills push heart rate up. Shorten your stride, lean slightly, and walk the steepest part if needed. Effort matters more than pace on climbs.
Week ten. My long run is 16 km. I got a blister on my right heel last time.
Heel blisters usually come from slipping. Try a heel-lock lacing pattern, thin moisture-wicking socks, and a bit of anti-chafe balm before the run. Tape the spot if it keeps coming back.
I've got the lacing sorted. Now I'm worried about the race itself. What pace should I target? My 10k time trial was 58:30.
A 58:30 10k suggests a half marathon of about 2:10 to 2:12, around 6:10 to 6:15 per km. Start the first 5 km slightly slower than that, then settle in and speed up after 15 km if you feel good.
I like having a plan. Can you outline the last four weeks, including the taper?

Week 13: 18 km long run. Week 14: 20 km, your longest. Week 15: 14 km and easy runs at normal length. Race week: two short easy runs, 20 minutes each, with strides on Thursday and rest the day before.
Race morning is going to be early. The start time is 8:30 and the venue is a 50-minute drive.
Plan to leave about two and a half hours before the start. Eat your usual breakfast three hours before, hydrate gently, and arrive early enough for toilets and a 10-minute warm-up jog.
What should I wear? It might be cold in March.
Dress as if it were 10°C warmer than the forecast. Wear a throwaway layer to the start line, run in shorts or tights you've already trained in, and nothing new on race day.
Got it, nothing new on race day. I do worry about sleeping badly the night before.
The night two nights before matters most. Aim for a normal bedtime two nights out, keep the day before relaxed, and lay your kit out early so there is nothing to stress about.
I've also been cross-training. Is swimming a good substitute for a missed run?
Swimming is a fine low-impact option on rest days or when injured, but it doesn't replace running-specific load. Use it as extra aerobic work, not as a swap for a long run.
Understood. How should I recover after the race?
Walk, eat, and drink right after. Take two or three easy days, then gentle runs. Expect stiff quads for a few days; a short walk each day helps more than complete rest.
And what should I do about the knee if it flares up again before the race?
Back off immediately, ice it after activity, keep the hip exercises going and avoid long downhill running. If it hurts walking down stairs or doesn't ease in a week, get it checked.
I'm building three raised beds, each 3 metres by 1.2 metres, in a sunny corner of the garden. What soil mix should I fill them with?
A good mix is about 60% topsoil, 30% compost and 10% coarse sand or grit for drainage. Fill the beds in layers and water each layer so it settles.
My soil test says the pH is 7.4. Is that okay for vegetables?
Most vegetables prefer a pH of 6.0 to 7.0, so 7.4 is slightly high. Adding sulphur or lots of compost lowers it slowly. Blueberries would struggle, but brassicas tolerate alkaline soil well.
I want to grow tomatoes, courgettes, runner beans and some salad. Which goes where?
Put tall plants like beans and tomatoes on the north side of each bed so they don't shade the rest. Courgettes need space, so give them a whole corner. Salad crops fit in the gaps.
Last frost here is usually around May 10. When should I start tomatoes?
Sow tomato seeds indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, so about mid-March. Harden the seedlings off for a week and plant out after May 10 once nights stay above 8°C.
I picked a cherry variety called Sungold and a beefsteak. How far apart should I space them?
Space cordon tomatoes about 45 cm apart with 60 cm between rows. Sungold is a cordon type, so tie it to a cane and remove the side shoots weekly.
The seedlings are leggy and falling over on my windowsill. What went wrong?
Leggy seedlings usually mean too little light. Move them to a south-facing sill or add a grow light 10 cm above the leaves for 14 hours a day, and bury the stems deeper when you pot them on.
Planted out on May 14. A week later slugs ate half of my young bean plants overnight.
Slugs love young beans. Use wool pellets or copper tape, water in the morning, not the evening, and go out with a torch after dark to collect them. Beer traps work but attract more slugs.
Wool pellets are down. How often should I water the beds in summer? I have a hosepipe and a water butt.
Water deeply twice a week rather than a little every day, in the morning. Tomatoes and courgettes need about 5 litres per plant per watering in hot weather. Mulch with straw to hold moisture.
Mulched with straw. The tomato leaves now have brown blotches with yellow rings. Is that blight?
Brown blotches with yellow halos suggest early blight, an infection called Alternaria. Remove affected lower leaves, keep foliage dry, water at the base, and do not compost the diseased leaves.
Removed the bad leaves. I also have basil. Does it really help tomatoes?
Basil is a popular companion and may deter some pests, though evidence is mixed. It is certainly a good use of space and tastes great with tomatoes. Plant it at the base of each tomato.
I planted basil. Now the courgettes are huge and I get four a day. What do I do with all of them?
Pick them small, at around 15 cm, to keep the plant producing. Grate and freeze for bread, make fritters, pickle them, or give some to neighbours. A glut is normal.
I'll make fritters. Pigeons are also pecking my cabbages. Any non-chemical fix?
Net them. Use a 2 cm mesh on a frame so birds can't reach through, and secure the edges with pegs. Reflective tape helps only for a short time.
Netting is up. My runner beans have flowers but they're dropping without setting pods.
Flower drop in beans is usually dry soil or hot nights. Water more often at flowering, mist the flowers lightly in the morning, and pick pods young to keep new ones coming.
Watering more helped. In August I want to sow something for autumn. What can go in now?
In August sow salad leaves, spinach, radishes, pak choi and winter lettuce. Sow carrots until mid-July. Cover with fleece when nights drop below 5°C.
Sowed spinach and pak choi. How do I rotate crops next year so the beds stay healthy?
Use a three-bed rotation: legumes, brassicas and roots or fruiting crops move one bed along each year. Tomatoes should not follow tomatoes or potatoes, because disease carries over in the soil.
Draw me a rotation plan for my three beds. Bed A had tomatoes and basil, B had beans and courgettes, C had salad and cabbages.

Next year: A takes beans and peas, B takes brassicas such as cabbage, and C takes tomatoes, courgettes and basil. The year after, shift again so that each bed rests from the same family for three years.
That works. How do I save seeds from my best tomatoes?
Choose a ripe fruit from your healthiest open-pollinated plant, scoop out the seeds with the gel, ferment in water for 3 days, rinse, and dry on a plate. Hybrid varieties don't come true.
Sungold is an F1 hybrid, isn't it? So I shouldn't save those seeds.
Correct, Sungold is an F1 hybrid, so saved seeds give unpredictable plants. Buy fresh seed for it each year, and save seeds from the beefsteak if it's an heirloom.
It is an heirloom. Last question: how do I protect the beds over winter?
Cover empty beds with cardboard and a thick layer of compost, or sow green manure like field beans or clover. This protects the soil from rain, feeds it, and suppresses weeds.
Green manure it is. Should I add lime to the beds before sowing, given my high pH?
No, don't add lime. Your pH is already above neutral. Skip lime and sulphur; compost alone will keep the beds balanced, and recheck the pH in spring.

I'm building a signup form in React with TypeScript. It has email, username, password and a terms checkbox. I keep a separate useState for each field and it's getting messy. Is there a better pattern?

Yes. Either one useReducer for the whole form, or a library like react-hook-form. A reducer keeps the logic in one place; react-hook-form also cuts re-renders because inputs are uncontrolled by default.
I want to avoid a library for now. Show me the reducer approach.

Keep state as { values, errors, touched, status }. Dispatch actions such as changed, blurred and submitted. The reducer updates values on change and marks a field touched on blur, so errors only show once the user has left the field.
Where should the validation functions live? I put them inside the component but it's long.
Move them to a validators.ts file as pure functions that take a value and return an error string or undefined. They are then easy to unit test and reuse on the server.
OK. My username needs to be unique. I call /api/username-available on every keystroke and it hammers the server.

Debounce it. Write a useDebouncedValue hook that waits 400 ms after the last keystroke before returning the value, and only call the endpoint when the debounced value changes and passes local validation.
I wrote useDebouncedValue with a setTimeout inside useEffect. Sometimes an old response overwrites a newer one, so the wrong message shows.
That's a race condition. Use an AbortController: abort the previous request in the effect's cleanup, or keep a request id and ignore any response that isn't the latest.
I used AbortController. Now the password field. What rules are reasonable?
Require a minimum length of 12 characters, allow all characters, and check against a list of common passwords instead of forcing symbols. Show a strength hint but don't block on it.
Should I show the password rules before the user types or only after an error?
Show the rule up front as helper text, for example 'At least 12 characters', and turn it into an error message only after blur or a failed submit. People hate guessing requirements.
Makes sense. How do I make the error messages accessible to screen readers?
Give each error element an id, link it with aria-describedby on the input, set aria-invalid when there is an error, and use role=alert for the summary at the top of the form after a failed submit.
My terms checkbox label isn't clickable. It's a span next to the input.
Use a real label element with htmlFor matching the input id, or wrap the input inside the label. Then clicking the text toggles the checkbox and screen readers announce it properly.
Fixed. Now submission: I disable the button while the request is pending but users can still press Enter and submit twice.
Guard in the handler, not just the button. If status is 'submitting', return early. Better, also send an idempotency key with the request so the server ignores duplicates.
I'll add the guard. What should happen on a server validation error, like email already registered?
Return field-level errors in a consistent shape, such as { errors: { email: 'Already registered' } }, dispatch them into the reducer, focus the first invalid field and announce the summary.
Focus the first invalid field: how, with refs?
Keep a ref map keyed by field name. After dispatching the errors, in an effect that runs when the errors change, find the first field with an error in your field order and call focus() on its ref.
Works. I want to add an avatar upload with a preview. The file is up to 2 MB.
Validate type and size in the change handler before reading it. Use URL.createObjectURL(file) for the preview and revoke it in cleanup with URL.revokeObjectURL to avoid leaking memory.
How do I test all this? We use Vitest and Testing Library.

Test behaviour: type into the fields with userEvent, blur, and assert on error text by role. Mock fetch for the username check, use fake timers to advance the 400 ms debounce, and assert the last response wins.
Could you give me a test for the debounce part specifically?
Use vi.useFakeTimers(), type 'abc', advance 399 ms and expect no call, advance 1 ms more and expect exactly one call to /api/username-available with 'abc'. Restore real timers in afterEach.
Next, I'd like to persist the draft of the form in case the user reloads.
Save values (never the password) to sessionStorage in a debounced effect and load them as the reducer's initial state. Clear the draft after a successful submit.
Why not the password? It's just a draft.
Storage is readable by any script on the page, so a stored password could be stolen by an XSS bug. Let the browser's password manager handle it; leave the field empty on reload.
Fair. Separately, the form is slow on my old phone. Typing in the email field lags.

Check what re-renders. Memoize the field components with React.memo, pass stable callbacks, and avoid creating objects in props. Use the React Profiler to see which components render on each keystroke.
The Profiler shows the whole form re-rendering. The avatar preview is the heaviest.
Move the preview into its own memoized component that only receives the object URL. Compute nothing heavy during render, and decode large images with a smaller thumbnail.
That fixed most of the lag. Last thing: should the form be one page or a multi-step wizard?
For four fields a single page converts better. Use steps only when the form is long or branches. If you do add steps, keep the URL in sync so back and forward work.
I want to build a household budget spreadsheet. Two of us, my flatmate and me, split rent 60/40 because my room is bigger. Rent is 1,450 a month. Where do I begin?

Start with one sheet for transactions and one for the monthly summary. On the transactions sheet use columns for date, description, category, amount and who paid. The summary sheet will total by category and by person.
Which categories should I use? I don't want fifty of them.
Keep it to about ten: Rent, Utilities, Groceries, Transport, Eating out, Subscriptions, Health, Fun, Savings and Other. You can always split a category later if one grows too large.
Good. My bank exports a CSV with dates like 03/11/2026 and amounts with a comma as the thousands separator, so the spreadsheet treats them as text.
Set the locale to match the export under File settings, or convert with DATEVALUE and VALUE after SUBSTITUTE removes the commas. Do the clean-up on an import sheet and keep the raw data untouched.
I'll use an import sheet. How do I sum transactions by category for one month?
Use SUMIFS: =SUMIFS(Transactions!E:E, Transactions!C:C, A2, Transactions!A:A, ">="&B1, Transactions!A:A, "<"&EDATE(B1,1)) where A2 is the category and B1 is the first day of the month.
That works. How can I show what my flatmate owes me for shared bills?
Add a Shared column to transactions. Compute each person's share with the 60/40 split, subtract what each already paid, and the difference on the summary sheet is who owes whom.
Our electricity is on a direct debit in my name, 96 a month, and the internet is 38 a month in my flatmate's name.
Then you pay 96 and she pays 38 up front, but both are shared at 60/40. Total shared is 134, your share is 80.40, hers is 53.60, so she owes you 42.40 on utilities.
Great. Now subscriptions. I have a lot of annual ones that hit once a year.
Create a sinking fund: list each annual cost, divide by 12, and move that amount to a savings pot monthly. Then the budget shows a steady monthly cost instead of a surprise in one month.
I have six annual subscriptions totalling 420 a year. So 35 a month?
Exactly. Add a row on your monthly summary called Sinking fund: subscriptions with 35, and transfer it into a separate savings pot on the same day each month.
How big should my emergency fund be? My essential spending is about 2,100 a month.
A common target is three to six months of essential spending, so 6,300 to 12,600 for you. Start with one month, 2,100, then build to three months.
I'll aim for three months, 6,300. I can put aside 400 a month. How long will that take?
6,300 divided by 400 is 15.75, so about 16 months. If you can raise it to 500 a month you'd reach it in 13 months.
Can the sheet calculate that automatically? Target, monthly saving and months left.
Yes. Put the target in B1, current balance in B2, monthly saving in B3, and use =ROUNDUP((B1-B2)/B3,0) for months left. Add EDATE(TODAY(), months) to show the finish date.
I'd like the overspent categories to turn red automatically.
Use conditional formatting with a custom formula: select the Actual column and apply =C2>B2 where B is the budget and C is actual, with a red fill. Add amber when it reaches 90% of budget.
Done. Next: how do I carry unspent money over to next month for some categories like Fun?
Add a Rollover column: last month's budget minus actual, only for categories you mark as rollover. Next month's available amount is the budget plus rollover, using IF to skip other categories.
I want a chart of spending by category for the year. Pie or something else?
Prefer a horizontal bar chart sorted descending. Pies are hard to compare when you have ten slices. Use a pivot table of category by month as the data source and filter out Savings.
Pivot table done. How do I stop making typos in the category column?
Use data validation with a dropdown list pointing to a named range called Categories. Reject invalid entries so only the ten categories can be used.
Named ranges are neat. Can I use XLOOKUP to auto-fill the category based on the description, like a shop name always being Groceries?
Make a Rules sheet with keywords and categories, then use =IFERROR(XLOOKUP(TRUE, ISNUMBER(SEARCH(Rules!A:A, B2)), Rules!B:B), "Other") as an array formula. New merchants fall back to Other.
Do I need to protect the formulas so my flatmate doesn't overwrite them?
Yes. Protect the summary and rules sheets and leave only the transactions input columns editable. Give your flatmate edit access to those ranges only.
She keeps forgetting to log her cash purchases. Any trick?
Add a mobile-friendly web form that appends rows to the transactions sheet, and set a weekly reminder. Keep the form to three fields: amount, category and note.
Also, it's tax season soon. Can I tag expenses I can claim for my home office?
Add a Tax column with a dropdown (Deductible, Not deductible) and a note for the receipt. Then SUMIFS the deductible rows by year and keep scans of receipts in a folder named by year.
Last question: how often should I review the budget?
A ten-minute weekly check to log transactions, and a longer monthly review to compare budget versus actual, adjust categories and move the sinking fund and savings transfers.
I have a monthly sales export at /data/exports/sales_2026-10.csv that I clean by hand in a spreadsheet. I want a Python script instead. It has about 200,000 rows. Where do I start?
Use pandas. Read the file with pd.read_csv, pass dtype for columns that must stay strings like order_id, and parse_dates for the date column. Then do cleaning steps as small functions you can test.
It fails right away with UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x93 in position 4121.
Byte 0x93 is a curly quote in the cp1252 code page, so the file isn't UTF-8. Pass encoding='cp1252' to read_csv. If you're unsure of an encoding, the charset-normalizer package can guess it.
cp1252 worked. The amount column is strings like '$1,204.50' and some are blank.
Clean with str.replace(r'[$,]', '', regex=True), then pd.to_numeric(errors='coerce'). Blank or malformed values become NaN, which you can count and log before deciding to drop or fill them.
There are duplicate orders because the export overlaps by a day each month. How do I remove them?
Use df.drop_duplicates(subset=['order_id'], keep='last'). Keep the last in case a later export corrected an earlier row. Log how many rows were removed so a sudden jump gets noticed.
Customer names have trailing spaces and inconsistent case: 'ACME ltd', 'Acme Ltd '.
Normalise with str.strip() and str.title(), but keep the original in a separate column if you need an audit trail. For matching, compare lowercase versions rather than the display value.
Dates come in two formats, 2026-10-03 and 03/10/2026. parse_dates gave warnings.

Parse explicitly. Try pd.to_datetime(col, format='%Y-%m-%d', errors='coerce') first, then fill the remaining NaT values with a second pass using format='%d/%m/%Y'. Never let pandas guess day-first versus month-first.
Good point. How should I structure the script? Right now it's one 300-line file.
Split into read, clean and write functions, plus a main() that wires them together. Put config such as paths in one place, and use argparse so the file path is an argument rather than hard-coded.
I'll use argparse. I also want logging instead of print statements.

Use the logging module with a basicConfig in main(): level INFO, a timestamped format, and a file handler writing to /var/log/sales_clean.log. Log counts at each step: rows read, rows dropped, rows written.
Where should the cleaned output go? I want it to be loaded into our reporting database.
Write to a new file with a date in its name, such as /data/clean/sales_2026-10.parquet, first to a temp file and then rename it, so a half-written file never gets picked up.
Parquet or CSV for the output?
Parquet. It keeps types, so dates stay dates and amounts stay numbers, it is much smaller, and it loads faster. Use CSV only when another tool can't read Parquet.
I'll go with Parquet. I want this to run automatically on the 2nd of every month at 02:15.
Use cron: 15 2 2 * * /opt/etl/venv/bin/python /opt/etl/clean_sales.py --month previous. Use absolute paths and the virtualenv's interpreter, since cron has a minimal environment.
What should the script do when the input file is missing?
Exit with a non-zero status and a clear log message. Cron mails or monitoring can then flag it. Use distinct exit codes, for example 2 for missing input and 3 for validation failure.
Add validation too: the cleaned data should have no negative quantities and every order should have a date.
Write a validate(df) function that raises with a summary if any check fails: negative quantity, null order_id, or null date. Fail before writing output, never after.
How do I test the cleaning functions without the big CSV?
Use pytest with tiny DataFrames built inline. One test per cleaning rule: the currency string, the two date formats, the duplicate order, and the whitespace in the names. Use tmp_path for file tests.
Can you give me a pytest for the date parsing?
def test_dates(): s = pd.Series(['2026-10-03', '03/10/2026', 'bad']); out = parse_dates(s); assert out.iloc[0] == out.iloc[1] and out.isna().iloc[2]. Both formats should give 3 October 2026.
Tests pass. The script uses 1.8 GB of memory on the full file. Our server has only 2 GB.
Read in chunks with chunksize=50_000 and process each chunk, or cut memory by reading only needed columns with usecols and using category dtype for repeated strings.
I'll use usecols and category. Dedup across chunks is a problem though.
Deduplicate with a set of seen order ids, or sort first. With 200,000 rows, the simplest fix may be reading only order_id and date first to decide which rows to keep.
I'm going with usecols and category dtypes, memory is 600 MB now. Python version question: we're on 3.12, any reason to move to 3.13?
Not for this script. 3.12 is supported for years. Upgrade when a library you need requires it, and test in a fresh virtualenv with pinned requirements first.
Speaking of which, how should I pin dependencies?
Keep a requirements.in with top-level packages and compile it to a fully pinned requirements.txt with pip-tools, including hashes if you want. Install from that file in the cron virtualenv.
Last thing: if the job fails at 02:15 I want a message. Email?
Cron emails output to the local user if mail is set up, but a more reliable route is to call a small notify() function on failure that posts to a team chat webhook, and still exit non-zero.

messages.text: I wear glasses and get eye strain after long screen sessions.
The 20-20-20 rule can help: every 20 minutes look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
I get hay fever from May to July every year.
Pollen season, then. Showering before bed helps.
I don't own a car; I use a car club when I need one.
Car clubs are handy for occasional trips.
I'm travelling to the coast for a week in June.
Sounds great. Do you want help packing?
